title: Opinion | Are Nepal’s celebrated technocrats serving the country or global capital? - The Kathmandu Post
description: Opinion | Are Nepal’s celebrated technocrats serving the country or global capital?  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
There is a distinct, recurring theatre to economic governance in the Global South. Every few years, a polished, Western-educated technocrat emerges from the periphery, steps onto an international stage, and is bestowed a gleaming accolade by the high priests of global finance. In 2016, Ram Sharan Mahat was named Global and Asia-Pacific Finance Minister of the Year by The Banker , a publication nestled within the institutional embrace of the UK’s Financial Times. A decade later, Swarnim Wagle was thrust onto the TIME100 Climate list as a visionary leader navigating the existential perils of planetary heating.

On the surface, these honours are sold to the domestic public as triumphs of national, patriarchal pride. We are invited to celebrate the brilliance of our native sons who have conquered the boardrooms of internationally celebrated think tanks and academia, proving that a small, landlocked Himalayan republic can produce minds capable of swimming in the deep end of global statecraft.

Dive beneath the glittering surface, and a far more calculated, structural dynamic reveals itself. These awards are not dispassionate acknowledgements of technical genius. They are the ‘soft-power stamps of approval’ bestowed upon local stewards who ensure that when disaster strikes, the country remains safely anchored to the orthodoxies of the Western capital.

To understand the strategic function of this technocratic class, one must first dismantle the myth of the neutral technocrat. In international political economy, there is no such thing as an ‘unaligned’ economist. Every macroeconomic policy framework carries an ideology; every structural adjustment redistributes power, and the aligned economics aims to fulfil a very specific structural necessity for Western institutional governance. Global financial institutions like the IMF and the World Bank cannot impose policies directly on developing countries without triggering negative reactions and resistance. To avoid this, they rely on well-credentialed local economists who understand domestic politics. These leaders act as intermediaries, packaging Western economic models in local language and framing market-driven reforms as necessary, homegrown solutions.

During the 2015 earthquake recovery, the prevailing policy framework did not treat the disaster merely as a humanitarian imperative. It used the moment to embed market-oriented principles into the foundation of state response. Instead of relying on direct state-led construction, the recovery strategy outsourced housing and infrastructure to private contractors, non-governmental organisations, and market mechanisms. At the international donor conference, Nepal was positioned as a disciplined, market-friendly borrower, securing massive loan packages from the World Bank and Asian Development Bank that came bound to strict fiscal restraint and deregulation. By turning a national humanitarian emergency into an opportunity to expand public-private partnerships and privatised supply chains, Mahat effectively signalled that market-driven solutions were the only viable way forward for Nepal’s economy.

However, if every crisis is met by borrowing more from multilateral banks or adopting the latest Western policy trends, the state never builds its own internal muscle, sovereign financial reserves, or independent development model. The path of least resistance in the short term becomes a structural trap in the long term.

What seems interesting, though, is the operational genius of the ‘aligned economics’ that can be observed, especially in the moment of profound crisis. In Capitalism and Freedom , Milton Friedman penned the ultimate manual for neoliberal engineering: “Only a crisis, actual or perceived, produces real change. When that crisis occurs, the actions that are taken depend on the ideas that are lying around.” Nepal has served as a living laboratory for this exact dynamic twice in recent memory.

Following the 2015 earthquake, Finance Minister Mahat used the disaster to push market-friendly recovery policies and foreign loans. Today, Nepal’s main threat has shifted from sudden earthquakes to cascading climate disasters like flash floods, cloudbursts and landslides that destroy farms and infrastructure. In this updated framework, exemplified by Wagle’s inclusion on the TIME100 Climate list, environmental disruption is framed through the lens of global green finance. Here, the policy language evolves: ‘free markets’ give way to ‘carbon markets’. It is framed as a financial opportunity to connect Nepal to green bonds and UN climate funds.

Even though the vocabulary has changed from ‘free markets’ to ‘climate finance’, the playbook remains the same. When severe climate disasters destroy local communities and wreck the national budget, aligned economics does not ask for unconditional financial reparations. Instead, it uses the crisis to push modern market tools like carbon credits, green bonds and debt swaps. By framing these financial solutions as absolute necessities, it bypasses local democratic debate and ties countries like Nepal deeper into Western financial systems. Local stewards are named to prestigious lists essentially as a reward for keeping the country friendly to foreign capital. In the end, global summits offer Nepal plenty of praise and token promises but leave the country to pay multi-billion-dollar recovery bills almost entirely on its own.

Defenders argue that Nepal is too small and aid-dependent to afford ideological purity, needing ‘safe hands’ who can win respect in Western capitals, negotiate loans, and keep the country solvent. While this pragmatism sounds reasonable, it comes with a massive long-term cost. When a nation outsources its economic vision to technocrats who answer to foreign institutions rather than their own people, it triggers a series of devastating structural consequences.

Overt reliance on aid and the market prevents Nepal from building strong, independent public institutions. When outsiders manage disaster and climate projects, the local government loses its governing power, reducing the state to a clearinghouse for foreign programmes, and when global financial rules dictate economic decisions, elections become empty rituals of identity and patronage. A small circle of foreign-approved elites starts controlling the state.

title: Opinion | How Mamta Kafle case shows why digital records matter when a Nepali disappears abroad - The Kathmandu Post
description: Opinion | How Mamta Kafle case shows why digital records matter when a Nepali disappears abroad  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Before Nepali nurse Mamta Kafle Bhatt disappeared in Virginia, she sent her brother a photograph and asked him to preserve it. He later testified that it appeared to show an injury to her face and that she planned to delete it from her phone. On November 10, a Virginia jury convicted her husband, Naresh Bhatt, of her murder. The case was not a digital-inheritance dispute, and there is no reported evidence that her family was denied account access. It nevertheless illustrates why a digital record can matter long after it is shared.

What happens to other digital records when a Nepali abroad disappears or dies? A message may be potential evidence, a payslip may establish unpaid wages, and a photograph may be a family’s treasured memory. They may sit on the same phone or cloud account, but they do not call for the same kind of access.

There are four different routes through this problem. First, keep relevant material, along with its context, and seek advice before deleting, resetting or altering a device. In a suspected crime, families should contact the appropriate investigators promptly rather than try to enter an account without authority. Second, police and courts may seek relevant records using the legal powers available in the country concerned. Third, relatives or authorised representatives may ask a platform for particular information or account closure, subject to its rules and applicable law. Fourth, heirs may pursue money, property or other lawful entitlements without automatically gaining access to every private conversation.

What the platforms allow

In enquiries to major technology and messaging providers, I found differing approaches to deceased users’ accounts. Rakuten Viber provided detailed written answers: It has no digital-legacy or trusted-contact feature, and it cannot retrieve delivered end-to-end encrypted chats from its servers for relatives. In a further clarification, Viber said families can request closure of a deceased user’s account through its support form. Typical documents include a death certificate, the deceased user’s Viber number, proof of the requester’s legal authority, identification and contact details. Cross-border requests are considered case by case. Closure does not grant access to private messages; copies may separately exist on recipients’ devices or in backups.

Other services allow planning. Google’s Inactive Account Manager lets users choose trusted contacts and selected categories of data to share when an account becomes inactive. Apple’s Digital Legacy provides designated contacts access to eligible information but excludes passwords and passkeys in iCloud Keychain. Microsoft’s OneDrive Digital Legacy offers a trusted contact read-only access to OneDrive files, not control of an Outlook account.

Apple and Microsoft directed my enquiries to their published documentation; Google’s information comes from its public guidance. There is no universal right to inherit an account or its credentials, and procedures for deceased users are not the same as those used in criminal investigations.

Beyond an exceptional case

Consider a migrant worker who dies abroad leaving unpaid wages, insurance benefits or savings. The family may need a payslip or employment contract stored in an email account. Here the problem is not criminal evidence but a financial entitlement. The asset, the evidence needed to claim it and the account containing that evidence are not the same thing.

The objective should be to authenticate the claimant, not to make the claimant impersonate the deceased. Where possible, an employer or financial institution should verify a widow’s entitlement and provide the necessary records through an authorised process. She should not need her husband’s email password to establish what she is owed.

Nepal Police figures show that 1,401 bodies of Nepali migrant workers were repatriated in fiscal year 2024/25. That figure says nothing about digital-access disputes. It does, however, underline the scale of the administrative challenges families may face after a death overseas.

Choice before crisis

Insurance arrangements have made the idea of nomination familiar. Digital services should make it easier for users to nominate who may receive selected information after death, what may be shared and what should remain private.

Google, Apple and Microsoft already offer different forms of advance planning, but their controls vary. Someone might choose to share family photographs and employment documents while keeping private messages and passwords inaccessible. These choices should be easy to find, change or withdraw. Nomination would not transfer an account or automatically override encryption, another person’s privacy or applicable law. The principle is choice before crisis.

What Nepal can do

Nepal already has laws on succession, privacy and electronic transactions. The bigger challenge may be helping families navigate a fragmented system of records and institutions across borders.

Embassies and relevant agencies could give families simple guidance on preserving digital material in suspected-crime cases and contacting investigators. One public page could explain where families should turn for unpaid wages, insurance, bank balances and Foreign Employment Board assistance, and what documents they may need. Pre-departure orientation could also cover basic digital planning without encouraging password sharing.

Where existing law is sufficient, make the process clearer. Where genuine gaps remain, clarify the law. Nepal does not need a new law or agency for every digital problem.

For generations, Nepalis leaving for work abroad have prepared passports, contracts and emergency contacts. But our lives no longer fit entirely into folders and suitcases. When someone dies overseas, there may be wages to claim, records to locate and memories to preserve. When someone disappears, a photograph or message may matter for a very different reason.

title: Nepali negotiators at COP31 cling to hope for mountain agenda - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepali negotiators at COP31 cling to hope for mountain agenda  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
The joint proposal of Nepal and Bhutan tabled for COP31 negotiations has received a cold response from the parties, especially the rich nations that are unprepared to pay for loss and damage inflicted in mountainous countries as a result of climate change.

Proposals by Nepal and Bhutan, and separately by Kyrgyzstan, to secure formal agenda items on mountain-related issues at the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) failed to secure the backing of major negotiating blocs, according to Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal.

Speaking to the PTI news agency in Antalya, Türkiye, where the conference is going on, Khanal said the three countries would continue to face challenges in securing stronger formal recognition of mountain-related issues without the support of major countries.

Minister Khanal said some nations explicitly backed the proposals, while others remained reluctant. He did not name the countries but sources told the Post that a powerful bloc of nations had blocked the bid.

On Thursday in Antalya, Nepal, Bhutan, Kyrgyz Republic, Tajikistan and Pakistan hosted a joint discussion on the topic ‘Advancing the Mountain Agenda: Glaciers, Cryosphere and Resilience under Overshoot, Shared Responsibility and Sustainable Financing’.

The core objective of the event was to mainstream the agenda of the mountain countries adversely affected by the climate crisis.

Alongside faster access to finance for loss and damage caused by the adverse effects of climate change, Nepal is pressing for stronger recognition of mountain vulnerabilities in COP31 decisions during the ongoing UN climate conference.

The UN climate conference has to address issues ranging from funding to scientific research. Afterall, powerful countries have to fund for climate justice but they looked reluctant to do so, said the official familiar with the negotiations. There is a lack of diplomatic push and reach, according to the Nepali official.

The powerful nations reportedly have agreed to initiate dialogue on climate science and research but are largely uninterested in incorporating all demands and agendas put forward by Nepal and Bhutan.

Demands including predictable, accessible, and grant-based climate finance—not debt—for adaptation and resilient infrastructure and sustainable livelihoods are considered as tough to secure. Multi-hazard early warning systems with high-altitude glacier monitoring, satellite observation networks, and regional data sharing are other demands unlikely to be met as sought by Nepal and Bhutan, said officials.

Decisions at the UN climate negotiations require consensus among major and influential negotiating blocs. Although smaller and least developed countries backed Nepal’s proposal, it failed to secure support from influential developed countries and major negotiating groups.

Two major blocs play a decisive role in climate negotiations: the developed and wealthy countries, and the large grouping of developing countries and emerging economies known as the G77 and China.

The Umbrella Group represents developed countries including the United States, the United Kingdom, Japan, Australia, Canada and Norway. The US, however, has withdrawn from the process.

Developed and wealthy countries are concerned that recognising the Himalayas as a separate agenda item could eventually create pressure on them to provide billions of additional dollars in compensation and adaptation finance to mountain countries.

Officials said that Nepal's agenda is on the negotiation table and hope for some outcome when a document is finally adopted. Partial agendas and demands put forward by Nepal and Bhutan and backed by multiple countries will be inducted in the declaration, they said in a tone of cautious optimism.

Nepal and Bhutan’s proposal for a dedicated mountain agenda item was not formally adopted during preliminary negotiations, Foreign Minister Khanal confirmed in an interview with Anadolu News agency of Türkiye.

Türkiye holds the conference presidency, while Australia leads negotiations, with talks focused on turning climate pledges into action and strengthening support for developing countries.

“At this point, what we really want is the mountain issues to be recognised in the decision-making process,” Khanal said.

Nepal is seeking research and technical assistance to better understand warming and its consequences in mountain regions, giving communities more time to prepare for future disasters.

“Something will hopefully come in the outcome document as we are negotiating on various proposals,” Maheshwar Dhakal, joint secretary at the Ministry of Agriculture, Forest and Environment, told the Post from Antalya.

Nepal and Bhutan are pursuing ambitious mitigation measures for accelerating emission reductions consistent with the 1.5°C warming threshold, curb short-lived pollutants such as black carbon, and protect fragile mountain ecosystems.

Our melting mountains cannot wait for our negotiations to catch up with their changing reality, said Khanal.

“Some developed and advanced countries are trying to scuttle our bid,” another Nepali official told the Post from Antalya. “It's getting difficult for us to include our demands and agenda in the outcome document.”

Lawmaker Sagar Dhakal, who is participating in the negotiation process, has brought the situation out. At both the personal and institutional levels, “we made every effort to table and adopt the Mountain and Climate Change agenda,” Dhakal wrote on Facebook. “Developed countries repeatedly rejected the proposal, even after negotiations extended past 2:00am ahead of Monday’s COP opening.”

The agenda was then dropped from the negotiation paper, Dhakal wrote.

“Until money is there, we cannot address the challenges and crises faced by the mountain countries,” Arjun Karki, a CPN-UML lawmaker who is in Turkey attending the COP31, told the Post.

According to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, global financing needs to mitigate climate change are estimated at $5 trillion a year until 2030.

“Financing needs for climate action in developing economies alone are estimated at USD 2.4 trillion a year between now and 2030,” said the organisation that tracks global climate financing.

title: When is enough, enough? - Nepali Times
description: When is enough, enough?  Nepali Times
publisher.title: Nepali Times
full_article:
The Everest climbing industry has become so commercialised that we are all ho-hum about individual feats unless someone is summiting for the umpteenth time, or skiing solo down the world’s highest mountain.

This has never been truer than in the case of Melissa Arnot Reid, who has climbed Mt Everest six times as a guide, and is the first American woman to climb it without supplemental oxygen and make it back. Only six other women have done that.

Reid is a television personality and celebrity in her own right back home, and inspires young women and girls through public speaking engagements. She has written a confessional and introspective memoir, laying bare her soul. But the manuscript was originally not meant to be published as a book.

You can tell: it is full of character flaws of other people and herself, bad decisions and even a general lack of empathy. So, it is all there: everything that makes a person an extreme human.

Having had a difficult childhood in Colorado and Montana, especially due to her relationship with her mother. Reid took to climbing first as a form of escape that gradually turned into ambition to prove her self-worth. At 19, she started as a guide on Washington state’s Mount Rainier where she learned the business through some rocky personal choices and experiences.

PERSONAL BATTLES

This is a deeply personal story, full of lows and highs but more than mountaineering feats they are about human shortcomings, and how one internalises them to overcome flaws. So on the one hand, readers may find themselves rooting for her success on mountains while also not liking her very much as a person.

The author herself admitted to hating her younger self during the official launch of the book in Kathmandu in October. In that sense it is honest, frank and confessional. It is self-focused, and hence perhaps the word ‘self’ in the book’s title.

Reid came to Nepal for the first time in 2008 at 23 still seeking legitimacy. She climbed Everest in her the first attempt, and thereafter it was her sole focus to do it without supplemental oxygen which she finally managed in 2016.

title: The Nepali border villages that empty for six months every year - The Kathmandu Post
description: The Nepali border villages that empty for six months every year  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
As Nepal celebrated Tihar festival earlier this week, families across the country were preparing to reunite, decorate their homes with garlands of marigold and globe amaranth flowers, and exchange colourful tika. Even those who had been unable to return to their villages for Dashain were making plans to go home.

But for Anjani Bohara of Chhangru, a village on Nepal’s northwestern edge, the festive season was a time to leave home.

Before her family could move out, it had to store its harvest and make preparations for six months away. “There’s so much to do before we leave. We have to get everything in order, both at home and on the farm,” she said last week.

Her 13-member family was busy gathering firewood, cutting and drying fodder for livestock, and collecting dried leaves to use as bedding when they returned in April.

For six months each year, the long winter brings heavy snowfall and extreme cold to Tinkar and Chhangru. Snow remains on the ground for long periods, making life in either village difficult. To escape the harsh conditions, residents leave in November for Khalanga, the district headquarters of Darchula, and other lower-lying areas.

Because they will not return until April, families rush to complete their preparations before setting out. The seasonal migration, known locally as kuncha sarne , is an annual ritual, but leaving home still requires considerable work. Residents must store enough food, arrange care for their livestock, and prepare their fields so that farming can resume as soon as they return. Their houses remain locked and the villages deserted throughout the winter.

With the departure date approaching, residents are working round the clock to finish their tasks. In Chhangru and Tinkar, which lie along Nepal’s borders with China and India, few people can be found idle. Some are threshing buckwheat harvested in April and May. Others are tying napal , a Tibetan variety of wheat, into small bundles with their stalks intact before storing it. Some are setting aside potatoes, beans, flour, and other food for the winter, while others are making dried preserves from choto , a large variety of radish.

Every household must complete its farm work before leaving. “Most people have already brought in their crops. Now we will start carrying manure from the cattle sheds to the fields,” said Bhupendra Tinkari of Tinkar. “Once that is done, we will sow coriander and mustard greens. By the time we return, they will have sprouted and be ready to eat in April.”

Residents also sow garlic and peas before leaving. Manure piled in the fields now is spread over the soil after their return, before the next round of cultivation, Tinkari said.

Tinkar has 75 households and Chhangru 124, with a combined population of around 1,200. Both villages fall under ward 1 of Byas Rural Municipality in Darchula district. By mid-November, both will be completely deserted for the next six months.

“We may leave because of the cold, but we have to come back in the monsoon. That is why we must make arrangements not just for now but also for when we return,” said Hitesh Budhathoki, an elected member of ward 1 council of Byas Rural Municipality. “Getting everything ready before leaving makes things easier when we come back.”

Chhangru and Tinkar, both in the high Himalayas, have only one farming season a year. Livestock rearing is the main source of income for residents, and the animals also move with their owners during the seasonal migration.

The journey to the lowlands takes about a week on foot, through Indian territory.

“We take the milking cows with us wherever we go,” said Droupati Aitwal of Chhangru. “We leave the other animals at places along the route where there is good grazing, under the care of herders. We bring them back with us when we return.”

Families hire herders collectively and share the cost according to the number of animals each household leaves behind, she said.

The journey is particularly difficult for children, new mothers, pregnant women, elderly people, people with disabilities, and women travelling with livestock.

“It is difficult, but we have no option. This has been the practice since our great-grandparents’ time. We cannot stay in the villages because the snow and cold make it impossible,” Aitwal said.

Before setting out, each household performs rituals to worship its clan deity. Families invite the wider community and host feasts. A collective worship ceremony is held at the end, and residents leave the villages on the same day.

“We pray for the safety, well-being and prosperity of our families and community. Only after the worship is completed do we consider the preparations for departure formally finished,” said 80-year-old Devalal Budhathoki of Tinkar.

When families return around April, they unlock their houses and resume their routines. Garlic, mustard greens, coriander, and peas sown before their departure will have sprouted and be ready for tending. Farming, livestock rearing and village life gradually return to their usual rhythm. When winter comes again, the preparations to leave begin anew.

The cycle has continued in Chhangru and Tinkar for centuries.

But travelling through Nepal is far from easy. Landslides have damaged several stretches of the trail connecting Tinkar and Chhangru, while the mule track from Chhangru to Dumling is also in poor condition.

Residents say movement for both people and livestock is difficult because sections of the trail around Budi Khola, Mausyabhir, Ghatibagar, Dopkhe, Tambaku and Kaljul have been damaged.

Some sections of the route between Tinkar and Chhangru have been patched up with help from residents, the Armed Police Force and Nepal Police, but the trail remains far from fully repaired, Dan Singh Tinkari said.

The federal, provincial and local governments have spent money on repairing and rebuilding the mule track, but the problems persist. Four years ago, around Rs15.4 million was spent on the route, including Rs10.8 million through the Nepal Army, Rs3 million from the Sudurpaschim provincial government and Rs1.6 million from Byas Rural Municipality.

Yet the route remains difficult to use, forcing residents to continue travelling through India.

In previous years, residents were even held up in Khalanga when they tried to move their villages for the winter because of poor roads and problems at the border crossing. They staged a sit-in outside the District Administration Office, bringing their livestock with them.

For the Byansi community, the absence of a safe and reliable mule track has made the twice-yearly seasonal migration increasingly challenging.

The distance involved makes it difficult for the rural municipality to build a durable route using its own budget, said Dharam Raj Joshi, chief administrative officer of Byas Rural Municipality.

title: In Nepal, a minibus carrying 20 people plunged down a slope, killing 14 — Kathmandu Post - UA.NEWS
description: In Nepal, a minibus carrying 20 people plunged down a slope, killing 14 — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
In Nepal, a minibus travelling from Kathmandu fell about 700 metres down a slope near Chisapanigadhi in Bhimphedi Municipality, Makawanpur District. The crash occurred at around 5:45 a.m. on Thursday. Fourteen people — the driver and 13 passengers — were killed, the Kathmandu Post reports.

The vehicle, which had 14 seats, was carrying 20 people including the driver. According to police, seven injured people were taken to a hospital in Hetauda after the crash: two have already been discharged, two remain under treatment there, and three others were referred to a hospital in Bharatpur.

Possible causes of the crash

Police have not yet established the cause of the crash. Investigators are preliminarily considering the minibus being overloaded and driver fatigue after overnight work. According to their information, the vehicle transported passengers from Sarlahi to Kathmandu on Wednesday evening and set off again at around 2 a.m. on Thursday with passengers heading toward Hetauda.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Surviving passenger Sanjay Yadav suggested that the driver may have fallen asleep at the wheel. According to him, the minibus stopped in Chisapanigadhi and, when it resumed its journey, jolted sharply and fell down the slope. Ramesh Bista, head of the district traffic police in Hetauda, said the road at the crash site was wide and had no obvious hazardous features.

Crash investigation

The Makawanpur District Administration has formed a commission to investigate the crash. It is to determine the causes of the accident, assess the condition of the road and possible safety risks, and propose measures to prevent similar incidents. The commission was given seven days to prepare its report.

The 13 victims were residents of Sundarpur in Sarlahi District, where families were preparing for the Chhath festival. Most of them worked in the vegetable and fruit trade in Kathmandu.

title: Nepal prepares fourth amendment to land use rules — Kathmandu Post - UA.NEWS
description: Nepal prepares fourth amendment to land use rules — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
The Nepalese government is preparing the fourth amendment to the 2022 Land Use Regulations to temporarily ease restrictions on land parcel subdivision in local administrative units that have not completed land classification. Such transactions are currently suspended in 333 units. Kathmandu Post reports.

The Ministry of Land Management, Cooperatives, Federal Affairs and General Administration has already submitted the draft amendments to the Ministry of Finance for approval. After consent is obtained, the document is to be sent to the Ministry of Law, and it will take effect only after approval by the Cabinet of Ministers.

Classification completed by 420 units

According to the land ministry, only 420 of the country's 753 local administrative units have classified land according to the established categories. The 2019 Land Use Act requires local authorities to establish land use councils and conduct classification based on maps and data provided by the state.

The regulations provide for land classification into 10 categories, including agricultural, residential, industrial, forest and commercial areas, as well as areas for mineral extraction. In localities where classification has not been completed, transactions involving the subdivision of parts of plots have been restricted. At the same time, transactions involving entire plots, inheritance division, transfer of inheritance rights, transactions under court decisions, and deletion of records from the land registry are permitted.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Lack of funds and technical specialists

The government has repeatedly extended deadlines and temporarily eased restrictions, but after the deferrals expired, the bans returned. In September 2024, land administration services, including plot subdivision, were suspended in 620 local administrative units because only 133 of them had completed classification at that time.

President of the Municipal Association of Nepal Bhim Prasad Dhungana said that many municipalities lack funds and technical personnel. According to him, land classification costs at least 1.5 million to 2 million Nepalese rupees, while local authorities have not received sufficient funding from the federal and provincial governments.

The restrictions have affected developers and landowners who need to sell part of a plot to cover urgent expenses. President of the Nepal Land and Housing Development Federation Bishnu Ghimire noted that individual landowners suffer most from the suspension of transactions.

title: Nepali workers make a living on Kedarnath’s 22-kilometre trail - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepali workers make a living on Kedarnath’s 22-kilometre trail  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Kedarnath, in Uttarakhand’s Rudraprayag district in India, draws large numbers of pilgrims every year, including thousands from Nepal. But for many Nepalis, the Himalayan pilgrimage site is more than a religious destination. It is also an important source of livelihood.

Nepali workers are a familiar presence in the area, carrying pilgrims on their backs to the Kedarnath temple, transporting goods and running hotels and grocery shops. Their work becomes particularly lucrative during the months when the temple remains open.

Jeevan Bohara, 35, from Bungol Municipality-11 in Bajhang district, is among those who have made a living carrying the pilgrims. He has been doing the job in Kedarnath for 18 years, supporting his family with the income.

Bohara carries pilgrims who cannot make the steep climb to the temple. The journey from Gaurikund to Kedarnath is 22 kilometres on foot, and the steep terrain makes it difficult for many visitors to complete the trek on their own.

Workers charge according to the passenger’s weight. Bohara says they earn between 15,000 and 22,000 Indian rupees for carrying one person from Gaurikund to the temple.

A traditional carrier known as a kandi is used for the job. It is made by cutting away part of a basket and fitting it with cloth to create a seat. The passenger sits in the carrier, which the worker straps to his back. Only one person can be carried at a time.

A large number of Nepalis are engaged in this work, Bohara says.

Kamal Bag, 40, also from Bungol Municipality in Bajhang, has been carrying pilgrims in a kandi for the past 10 years. Despite the physical demands, he returns every year because the earnings are better than those available in other jobs in the area.

“The more work you do, the more you earn. Carrying people pays the most,” Bag said. “There are other jobs too, but they do not pay as well.”

Bag says a worker can save around 5,000 to 6,000 Indian rupees after carrying a pilgrim from Gaurikund to the temple and back. The savings can rise to 8,000 to 10,000 rupees when they get a well-paying passenger.

The journey from Gaurikund to the temple takes an entire day, he says. Food, accommodation and drinking water are expensive along the trail and at the temple, adding considerably to workers’ expenses.

Nepali citizens need several documents to work as pilgrim carriers in Kedarnath, Bag says. These include their citizenship certificate, a recommendation from the local village panchayat and an identity card issued by the police. The process costs around 4,000 to 5,000 Indian rupees.

Bag estimates that more than 2,000 Nepalis are currently working as pilgrim carriers in the Kedarnath area alone. Many others run hotels and grocery shops.

Some workers have already returned to Nepal for the Dashain festival. Those still working in the area will head home for Tihar or after the Kedarnath temple closes for the season.

The temple generally opens on Akshaya Tritiya in April and remains open until Bhai Tika, which falls in late October or early November. It closes for the winter as temperatures drop and heavy snowfall sets in. The months when the temple is open also bring a large influx of pilgrims, creating seasonal employment opportunities for Nepali workers.

But the work is not without danger. Landslides and other accidents along the mountain route have repeatedly put workers’ lives at risk.

title: International cricketers fall in love with Nepal beyond TU Ground - The Kathmandu Post
description: International cricketers fall in love with Nepal beyond TU Ground  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Since its inaugural season, the Nepal Premier League has fulfilled a long-held dream for local fans—watching global cricket stars perform right at the home of Nepali cricket. Beyond the boundary ropes of Kirtipur, these international icons have been equally captivated by Nepal itself.

With the tournament’s third edition drawing global icons—from Australian opener David Warner to South Africa’s David Miller, West Indian all-rounder Andre Russell, and Bangladeshi star Shakib Al Hasan—the league has also served as an informal tourism showcase. Between high-pressure fixtures under the floodlights, visiting cricketers have traded their team jerseys for casual wear to explore Kathmandu Valley and beyond.

“What an experience. Woo!” Warner said in a selfie video, from the snow-capped mountains, he uploaded on his social media on November 4. The video has 477,000+ reactions on Warner’s Instagram.

He had taken a helicopter ride to the mountains and even had breakfast, watching the tallest peak in the world, Mount Everest.

Warner, who landed in Kathmandu on November 1, played his first match for Kathmandu Gorkhas on November 2—departing for only 16 runs against Karnali Yaks. Upon his return from the mountains, Warner smashed 44 against Biratnagar Kings and 66 against Lumbini Lions. While he could only manage a single in his last match of the season—against Chitwan on November 9—Warner helped his team win all four matches he featured and took the Gorkhas to the top of the points table before leaving.

“Nepal, you have absolutely blown me away,” Warner wrote on his Instagram on Thursday. “From the incredible hospitality to the passion for cricket, the breathtaking scenery and, most importantly, the beautiful people, this has been an experience I’ll never forget.”

“Thank you for welcoming me with open arms,” Warner, who has won the World Cups across the three formats of the game, added as he shared a reel of photos and videos he captured in the country. “Until next time, Nepal!”

Other overseas players from Kathmandu Gorkhas also reached the mountains. Jahandad Khan had posted photos of him and his teammates with Mount Everest as the backdrop.

“Foreign players do their research before going to a foreign country. So had Warner. He was aware of Mount Everest and we too wanted to take him there,” said Shrawan Bahadur Singh, operations head of Kathmandu. “We were also aiming to promote Nepal through Warner, whose one social media post works a lot.”

And it seems the mountains did play an extra role in making Warner say that he will return the next season as well.

“Warner was extremely happy after returning from the mountains,” said Singh. “He has even promised to come back next season. He said that he played in countries throughout the world, but none were as beautiful as Nepal.”

But not all of the 50+ overseas players signed by the eight franchises got the opportunity to land in between the snowy mountains. Many had to have a look from far, but they enjoyed it too.

For instance, Russell, the Caribbean all-rounder, was glad that he got a hotel room from where he could see Mount Everest.

“Apart from the results, I love Nepal,” Russell said in a video by the Kings. “I can say it is such a peaceful place. The people are beautiful, warm and welcoming. They are not too much in my face. They are chill. They kind of give me a bit of Caribbean vibes. And they love their cricket.”

Sikandar Raza of Zimbabwe, who is also the No 1 T20I all-rounder of the world, during his visit to Nagarkot with the Chitwan Rhinos squad. Photo: Sikandar Raza/Facebook

Similarly, Chitwan Rhinos squad , including world’s No 1 T20I all-rounder Sikandar Raza , also had a night out in Nagarkot. Lumbini also took their squad to Kulekhani. Karnali went to Lele.

Several players have shared their experience in Nepal through social media, post-match presentations, pre-match press conferences and other meet and greet events.

Shakib Al Hasan had shared a video of the view of the Kathmandu Valley from Godawari, Lalitpur, on October 31. Hasan was accompanied by the whole Pokhara squad.

Likewise, the NPL also saw other legends grace the tournament as guests. Shoaib Akhtar, the legendary Pakistani pacer, came as the guest of Himalaya Sports, while Irfan Pathan, the legendary Indian pacer who is an ambassador of Pokhara Avengers, graced the TU Ground on Thursday. Both, Akhtar and Pathan, shared that they loved Nepal.

The Nepal Tourism Board (NTB), the state-run national tourism organisation, has also shared the moments of global cricket icons’ visit to Nepal.

On November 3 and 4, the NTB shared photos of Warner and Russell in action at TU Ground, respectively.

“When cricket brings global sporting icons to Nepal, it creates more than excitement on the field,” the NTB wrote while posting Warner’s photos. “It brings people, cultures and countries closer, while giving the world another reason to discover Nepal.”

Likewise, sharing Russell’s photos, the NTB wrote , “Nepal is more than a sporting destination. It is an experience worth coming back for.”

Some players, including Jimmy Neesham and Miller, have also enjoyed playing golf in Kathmandu.

Speaking at a get-together by the Cricket Association of Nepal, in coordination with alcohol products, Neesham had shared that he enjoyed the golf course in Gokarneshwar.

Miller also said that he had a good time on the golf course.

“Nepal has been fantastic so far,” Miller, who was captaining Karnali, said during the toss on Thursday. “The people have been amazing and the support from the crowd at the ground has been brilliant.”

title: Nepal's Foreign Employment Stuck in Traditional Destinations Amidst New Opportunities - Ratopati
description: Nepal's Foreign Employment Stuck in Traditional Destinations Amidst New Opportunities  Ratopati
publisher.title: Ratopati
full_article:
Kathmandu. Foreign employment, considered the main backbone of Nepal's economy, has been revolving only around Gulf countries and Malaysia for the last three decades. Nepali workers are also being attracted to new and attractive destinations in the global market, especially European countries.

In search of attractive salaries, human rights guarantees, and a secure future, the number of Nepalis going to Europe is increasing day by day. However, as the government has not opened the way to go to new destinations through manpower companies institutionally, millions of youths are forced to fall into the trap of middlemen and human traffickers.

The impractical provisions of the Foreign Employment Act, the non-cooperation of embassies in demand letter authentication, and the conflict between the Ministry of Labor and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs have disrupted the entire cycle of foreign employment. While the government tries to evade responsibility by saying that businessmen have not explored new destinations, businessmen are angry, saying that the government does not authenticate the demand letters it brings.

Who is actually obstructing the institutional and safe sending of Nepalis to new destinations like Europe? Who is benefiting from the state's policy? What is its solution? Here is an edited excerpt of an interview conducted by Anish Mijar of Ratopati with Rajendra Bhandari, former president of the Nepal Foreign Employment Association, focusing on these contemporary issues:

Traditionally, Malaysia, Qatar, and other Gulf countries have long been centers for Nepali workers. Are we unable to move beyond this or unable to think beyond it? The government is saying that it should explore new destinations. What is the situation of new labor destinations and traditional destinations, and how should we proceed now?

You have raised a very correct and timely issue. Looking back at the history of foreign employment in Nepal over the last 30 years, most of our workers are going to traditional destinations. Earlier, more than 90 percent of the workforce went to Gulf countries, and even now, about 80 percent of workers are going to Dubai, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, Oman, Bahrain, and Malaysia.

If we do not explore alternatives, and if natural disasters, conflicts, or a contraction of employment opportunities occur in those countries tomorrow, our foreign employment will come to a halt all at once. It is certain that this will have a large and serious impact on the country's economy. Therefore, while maintaining traditional destinations, we must move towards new and safe destinations.

However, there are two main obstacles to going to new destinations like this. The first obstacle is our Foreign Employment Act. The second obstacle is the slow and disorganized way our bureaucracy works.

Especially for sending people institutionally, the Foreign Employment Act mandates that the demand letter must be authenticated by the Nepali embassy in the respective country. There are embassies in the Gulf and Malaysia. Authentication happens there, and people are going.

The emerging destination now is Europe. About 300,000 Nepalis have already reached about 40 countries in Europe, the Balkan area of Eastern Europe, and non-Schengen countries. Some countries do not have our embassy.

Japan is the second attractive destination, but our embassy there has stopped authenticating demand letters, citing a lack of resources.

What has been the result of this? With the institutional route closed, people have chosen a second path. Middlemen and human traffickers have started arranging settings for visit visas or personal visas. Traffickers are taking people to Europe after extorting millions of rupees. Ultimately, the fault lies with the state mechanism and the embassies. Our foreign ministry officials and ambassadors are more inclined to exacerbate problems and focus on procedures rather than solving them. The Ministry of Labor understands one thing. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs understands another.

If we send 300,000 people to Gulf countries, let's send only 100,000 to Europe. In Europe, the salary is double or triple that of the Gulf. 100,000 people will send remittances equivalent to 300,000. There is human rights there. There is a safe environment. One can learn new languages, cultures, and skills. However, due to our law and the misunderstanding of the bureaucracy, new destinations are being closed, and workers are being confined to the old destinations.

How many countries has the government legally approved for labor permits? What is the current actual situation of sending people institutionally and individually?

Our workers have reached about 180 countries for employment. Among them, 111 countries are open for institutional sending by policy.

However, even though 111 countries are open, we only have embassies in about 28 to 30 countries. The law requires authentication from the embassy. This means that businessmen cannot send people institutionally to countries outside those 28/30 countries.

People have reached 180 countries, but the legal route is limited to only 30 countries. The government's policy is promoting middlemen, brokers, and traffickers to send people. Manpower entrepreneurs who have deposited guarantees with the state and are ready to work with full responsibility under the state's shadow are not given a path. Brokers bring individual visas, make arrangements, and send people.

The conflict between the Ministry of Labor and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs is the root of this. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs remains stuck in its old format and ego. It does not work and delays files.

The Ministry of Labor tries to improve. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs obstructs. There is no sense of responsibility or sacrifice for the country in our bureaucracy. Currently, about 35 percent of people are going through individual channels.

It is natural for someone to go to Europe individually as a doctor or engineer, but a common youth from a village pays millions to a middleman and goes to Europe on an individual labor permit. If they are stranded tomorrow, that same embassy will have to look after them. This also shows the poor mentality of the bureaucracy.

As the attraction to European countries increases, workers are going by paying a lot of money. While exploring new destinations, how should the challenges that may arise in the future be managed?

As you said, looking at the latest data, there is a significant presence of Nepalis in countries like Romania, Bulgaria, Hungary, Poland, Portugal, Spain, Germany, Italy, Greece, and Malta. Last year alone, 33,000 Nepalis went to Romania.

The thinking of the Nepal government is narrow. They say that if people go to Europe, they will run away or hide. In the 26/27 Schengen countries, there is open border. Their labor laws, human rights, and regulations are the same. Wherever the worker goes, they are safe within Europe.

Our clear statement is that if people go to Europe, make manpower entrepreneurs responsible. We will send them. We will keep track of where that labor goes and their track record.

We are ready to take full responsibility. But the process doesn't even start; the embassy does not authenticate the demand letter. When the path is closed, middlemen seize the opportunity and extort a lot of money.

Can the state open embassies in all 180 countries? It cannot. Today is the era of e-diplomacy. Using technology, demand letters should be authenticated online, and a policy should be brought to make manpower entrepreneurs fully responsible.

The entrepreneur must take responsibility for the worker's working station, minimum wage, services as per the agreement, and security. There should be no complaints; if there are, the entrepreneur must pay compensation.

Even when we say we are ready to take responsibility, the government does not listen. And brokers who syndicate in Malaysia keep entering through loopholes in the bureaucracy, while the government remains a mute spectator? The situation has arisen where middlemen are stronger than the government. Due to the lack of willpower in the bureaucracy, we are forced to be confined to new destinations.

Developed countries in Europe probably only look for qualified, capable, or skilled people. Is it because we don't have such skilled manpower that the government is showing no interest?

No. This is a completely wrong understanding. The biggest factors here are the government's lack of willpower, vested interests, and the weak thinking of the bureaucracy.

The Nepal government and Germany signed an agreement to take technically skilled people to Germany. We also made labor agreements with Spain and Romania. But where is the work?

Even for demand letters from countries with state-level agreements that guarantee worker security, the embassy does not provide authentication. This is like an unprecedented chaos. This dual character of the government is making workers more insecure.

You mentioned technology and skills. Europe has high technology; they are developed. But they also have a severe labor shortage. They need everything from low-level labor to high-level technicians. They offer attractive hourly wages.

If we open the way, we can produce trained manpower according to their demand within Nepal itself. When the market opens up, youths will learn trade skills even to go to Europe.

And another important thing is that people who go abroad do not just send money (remittances); they also bring back skill remittances. Twenty to thirty years ago, only traditional farming was done in Nepal. But youths who went to Israel learned skills there and brought about a 'tunnel farming' and modern agricultural revolution in Nepal upon their return. Similarly, youths who go to Europe and America tomorrow, after becoming accustomed to their AI, robotics, and modern technologies, will bring that technology to Nepal upon their return.

Today, in the age of the global village, America's IT is controlled from Nepal. Therefore, instead of stopping people by saying they lack skills, we should teach them skills and send them, and utilize their skills for nation-building.

One thing is missing. The government says it is working, but the private sector has not proactively proposed that these countries are suitable and suggested how to work. There is an accusation that they have not shown the way to the government?

This is the biggest disease of our bureaucracy. Blaming others to hide one's own weaknesses. If Nepali workers have reached 180 countries today, it is not because the government found that path. They have reached there through the initiative and hard work of the private sector.

In the past, the ministry had brought a regulation that allowed online authentication of demand letters for countries without an embassy. Businessmen also paid revenue to the state by sending 4,000-5,000 people to countries like Europe and Romania. They brought demand letters, but later the government itself abolished that regulation. So, can it be said that businessmen did not bring proposals?

We have repeatedly said – open the authentication of demand letters for all 40 European countries. We are ready to send people to all 180 countries. We (entrepreneurs) are ready to take full responsibility for the security and services of all those workers sent. What is stopping the creation of strict laws for this?

What is stopping the creation of laws that hold entrepreneurs fully responsible and liable for fines if workers do not receive the agreed-upon salary and facilities after being sent by entrepreneurs? The government is afraid to take responsibility itself, and it also does not want to open the path by making businessmen responsible.

The need of the hour is to implement an e-diplomacy system. Embassies should handle matters for countries where they exist, and for countries without embassies, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs should directly authenticate online. Let's create a system where full responsibility is given to entrepreneurs and test it for at least six months or one year. How many problems and complaints will arise? There is no point in saying that the private sector did not bring destinations when the system and method are not even created.

In conclusion, I will say this – the private sector has been instrumental in getting Nepali workers to 180 countries. Now, the government should adopt an open mind and open policies and make manpower entrepreneurs fully responsible.

Nepalis can easily reach excellent and safe destinations around the world, not just traditional countries. This will enrich the country both economically and technically.

title: Communication Minister discusses expanding collaboration in IT sector with his counterparts - The Rising Nepal

Kathmandu, Nov 13: Minister for Information and Communications Dr. Bikram Timilsina discussed expanding bilateral cooperation in the field of information and communication technology with his counterparts from Qatar and Estonia.

Minister Timilsina, who had arrived in Doha to participate in the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) 2026 Plenipotentiary Conference (ITU PP–26), held a bilateral meeting with Qatar's Minister of Communications and Information Technology Mohammed bin Ali Al Mannai, stated a press release issued by the Nepali Embassy in Doha on Thursday.

During the meeting held at the Doha Exhibition and Convention Center on the sidelines of the conference, Minister Timilsina expressed gratitude to the Qatari government for providing relief materials to citizens affected by the devastating flood in the Bhotekoshi River on August 26.

He also recalled the state visit of Nepal by Qatar's Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani in April 2024, discussing the friendly relations and long-term friendship between the two countries. Additionally, he expressed happiness as the 50th anniversary of diplomatic relations between Nepal and Qatar approaches.

Highlighting the importance of the telecommunications sector for a country with Nepal's geographical diversity, Minister Timilsina lauded the progress Qatar has achieved in this field.

The press release stated that the meeting also discussed ways to expand cooperation and opportunities between the two countries in the field of information and communication technology.

Meanwhile, Minister Timilsina held a separate bilateral meeting with Estonia's Minister of Justice and Digital Affairs, Liisa-Ly Pakosta.

During the meeting, he noted that Nepal can learn a lot from Estonia's experience in technology development and digital transformation.

Both sides exchanged ideas on identifying potential areas of cooperation in information and communication technology, including telecommunications.

The Nepali Embassy in Doha stated that Minister Timilsina, who participated in various bilateral meetings and other important events during the ITU PP-26 conference, is scheduled to depart to Kathmandu from Doha tonight. (RSS)

title: Europe Emerges as New Hub for Nepali Migrant Workers Amidst Shifting Destinations - Ratopati
description: Europe Emerges as New Hub for Nepali Migrant Workers Amidst Shifting Destinations  Ratopati
publisher.title: Ratopati
full_article:
Kathmandu. It is the compulsion of Nepali youth to shed sweat in foreign lands due to the lack of sufficient employment opportunities in Nepal.

While the Gulf countries were once the primary and sole choice for Nepali workers, labor destinations have started to change recently. Due to security and low wages, European countries are increasingly becoming new destinations as alternatives to Gulf countries.

Various European countries are becoming the choice of Nepalis due to good salaries, attractive benefits, social security, and perceived safety from a human rights perspective.

Immigration experts say that although Nepalis are rushing to go to Europe by paying more than to Malaysia and the Gulf, the government's preparation and regulation to manage this growing attraction towards Europe appear very weak.

They state that due to various problems arising in traditional labor destinations like the Gulf countries and Malaysia, Nepali workers' attraction has recently increased towards European countries.

Experts say the government has completely failed to search for new and safe labor destinations and to formally manage them. As the government makes no diplomatic efforts to find new destinations, workers are forced to take risks and go through informal channels, relying on agents and the private sector.

According to immigration expert Meena Poudel, old destinations like the Gulf and Malaysia are currently in disarray. She says that workers who gained skills working in the Gulf are looking for better jobs and alternatives, making Europe a center of attraction. However, the government's presence in opening up new destinations like Europe is almost nil.

“Currently, the most chaotic, jobless, and disorganized ministry is the Ministry of Labor. Neither have old agreements been renewed, nor have formal agreements been made to open pathways to Eastern European countries like Greece, Malta, and Cyprus,” Poudel said. “In the name of formal initiatives, there has been no meaningful diplomatic effort beyond inviting ambassadors for tea.”

Another immigration expert, Dr. Ganesh Gurung, also states that the government, and especially the Foreign Employment Board, has completely failed in searching for new markets. He pointed out that there has been no study on which countries in the global market need what kind of manpower and what kind of manpower Nepal possesses.

“Nepal is currently sending people wherever there is demand, which has branded Nepal as a country sending unskilled labor to the global market,” said Dr. Gurung. “The state has not focused on how to make our unskilled manpower earn more money by providing short-term training.”

Expert Gurung believes that Nepali embassies abroad should strategically search for markets to see in which sectors and how their citizens can be utilized, but this has not happened.

Experts conclude that foreign employment will always remain chaotic and risky until the state adopts a policy of training workers according to the demand of destination countries through diplomatic initiatives and sending them through formal channels.

Over 4.3 Million Nepalis Emigrated in 6 Years

The government has opened 111 countries for foreign employment. Nepalis are working in more than 178 countries through personal initiative and other means.

Looking at the statistics of the last six years, the trend of Nepalis going abroad is alarming. During this period, 2,673,419 people went for foreign employment after obtaining their first work permit. In the same period, 1,653,229 people obtained re-work permits. In the last six years alone, 4,326,648 Nepalis have gone for foreign employment.

In the fiscal year 2082/083 alone, 792,187 people went for foreign employment after obtaining work permits from the Department of Foreign Employment. Among them, 697,096 are male and 95,091 are female.

Compared to 839,266 people who obtained work permits in the fiscal year 2081/82, 47,079 fewer Nepali workers went abroad last year.

Europe is Becoming a New Hub for Nepalis

Many Nepalis still go to the six Gulf Cooperation Council countries – Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and UAE – and Malaysia, which are considered traditional labor markets.

According to the Department of Foreign Employment, 55.4 percent of workers still go to the Gulf region and 15.9 percent to Malaysia. However, amidst the tension and employment crisis in West Asia, Europe has emerged as a strong alternative.

Last year's statistics show a surge in Nepalis going to Europe. Last year, more than 80,000 Nepali workers went to Europe in search of employment.

In the last six years, 101,656 Nepalis have gone to work in European countries. The graph of those going to Europe is rising every year. While 5,134 people went to Europe in fiscal year 2077/078, the number increased to 21,896 in 2078/079, 21,984 in 2079/080, 24,067 in 2080/081, and in 2081/082, more than 80,000 Nepalis went to 29 out of 44 European countries.

According to the department's total statistics, in the first three months of the current fiscal year, a total of 792,187 people, including new and re-work permits, have received approval for foreign employment. Among them, 697,096 are male and 95,091 are female.

Europe's share of the total work permits has increased from 10.5 percent to 14.7 percent. According to the department, from Saun 2082 to Jeth 2083, 367,000 people have obtained new work permits for 160 countries.

Which European Countries Have How Many Gone?

According to the department's data, among European countries, Romania is the first choice for Nepalis, and Cyprus is the second. Demand for Nepalis has increased in agriculture, construction, hospitality, and manufacturing sectors in Eastern and Central European countries.

Last year alone, Romania accounted for the largest share (about 46 percent) of Nepalis going to Europe. 33,920 Nepali men and 4,111 women went there. Romania had allocated a quota of 100,000 for non-European workers, among whom Nepalis are the largest number among the 51,000 foreigners registered around Bucharest.

Other major destinations include Cyprus with 11,069 people (3,972 men, 7,097 women), Croatia with 7,662 people (6,284 men, 1,378 women), Malta with 6,110 people (4,589 men, 1,521 women).

Similarly, 3,800 went to Portugal, 3,788 to Serbia, 3,679 to Bulgaria, 3,126 to Greece, 2,650 to Poland, and 2,639 to Austria. Additionally, 1,724 went to Slovakia, 1,348 to the UK, 1,355 to Moldova, and 1,191 to Slovenia for employment.

The statistics for Cyprus are quite interesting. While the number of men is higher in other countries, the number of women in Cyprus is almost double that of men. The department stated that 7,097 women went to Cyprus due to high demand as caregivers and domestic workers.

According to government data, more than half of the total 792,000 workers who went for foreign employment last year are skilled workers. According to the department, there are 482,643 skilled workers, 190,264 unskilled, 114,614 semi-skilled, 3,570 professionals, and 1,096 highly skilled workers. While unskilled workers mostly go to the Gulf, a large number of those going to Europe have acquired skills.

Nepalis Going to Europe in the Last Five Years

Role of the Private Sector and Risks of Individual Work Permits

Currently, the government does not have a system for institutional work permits through manpower companies to European countries. However, the private sector is sending workers to European countries through informal channels.

Due to the absence of an institutional system, workers obtain individual work permits or go to Europe on visit visas through manpower company arrangements. The department's data shows a decrease in the number of people going through manpower agencies. While manpower agencies sent 359,675 people the previous year, they sent only 268,990 last year, a decrease of 90,685.

On the other hand, 128,520 people went on individual work permits last year, while 8,197 went through G2G.

Also Read ‘Government signs labor agreements, but embassies don't verify demands’

Due to the closure of institutional channels, manpower companies are charging workers between 1 to 1.5 million rupees in the name of sending them to Europe. Due to weak regulation, workers are facing severe financial exploitation and risks.

The president of the Nepal Association of Foreign Employment Agencies, Dik Bahadur Khatri, said that the government must immediately resolve the policy issue of demand letter attestation to send workers to new labor destinations like Europe as an alternative to West Asia and Malaysia.

He stated that employment opportunities in traditional labor destinations are shrinking due to war and monopolies, and demanded that the government open pathways to emerging destinations like European countries. He also mentioned that the private sector has played an important role in finding new labor destinations so far.

According to President Khatri, concentrating the labor market in only one region, West Asia and Malaysia, has led to serious impacts on foreign employment due to occasional legal complications, wars, and natural disasters.

“Currently, due to the ongoing war in West Asia, the demand for workers from there has decreased by about 27 percent. Malaysia is also disturbed due to syndicates,” said President Khatri. “Therefore, we need to expand the labor market. We should not delay in expanding and attesting new destinations like Schengen, non-Schengen, Balkan corridors, and Japan's SSW.”

Khatri said that although Nepali entrepreneurs are ready to send workers to new destinations like Europe, obstacles are being created due to government policies.

This problem started in 2075 BS when Section 15 (Cha) of the Foreign Employment Act, 2064, was amended to make it mandatory to get demand letters attested by the Nepali embassy in the respective country. “In the past, embassies in Europe like Germany, Austria, France, and the UK used to attest demand letters. But this has been completely stopped for the last 3 years,” he said.

Khatri informed that he is also a member of the committee formed by the Ministry of Labor to amend the flawed sections of the Act, and this issue has been prioritized there. However, he emphasized that the Ministry of Foreign Affairs holds the key to demand letter attestation and that the Ministry of Foreign Affairs should show promptness in this matter.

Khatri stated that the issue of demand letter attestation has been given high priority in the 15-point demands recently raised by entrepreneurs, and the government has been well-informed about it.

“Unless the knot of demand letter attestation is untied, we cannot expand to other labor markets. The government must take immediate steps in this regard,” he said.

Government Preparation and Diplomatic Obstacles in Finding New Destinations

The government has taken policy initiatives to find new labor destinations as an alternative to Gulf countries, but the implementation aspect is weak. The government has put forward a policy in its 2081/082 program to search for more destination countries, make labor audits mandatory, and provide pre-departure orientation training for free.

Nepal has currently signed labor agreements with Qatar, UAE, South Korea, Bahrain, Japan, Israel, Jordan, Malaysia, and Mauritius.

The government has been preparing for agreements with Maldives, France, Seychelles, and Qatar for a long time. The process of sending workers through government-to-government (G2G) channels to countries like the UK, similar to South Korea and Israel, is underway.

However, government facilitation for Europe is not effective. Due to the inability to get demand letters from Europe attested, workers cannot be legally sent through manpower agencies.

The then Minister of Labor, Sharad Singh Bhandari, had introduced a procedure whereby if the mission did not attest within 15 days, the department itself would do so. However, this matter has been left unresolved due to the conflict between the Ministry of Labor and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the change of government.

According to immigration expert Poudel, finding new destinations should be done at the diplomatic and political level, but instead, the government is only intimidating and taking action against manpower companies.

This has demoralized the private sector. Poudel states that since immigration policies are becoming stricter in Europe and Nepalis have to compete with unemployed citizens there, the private sector alone cannot manage the European market without government initiative.

Similarly, according to another expert, Dr. Gurung, although the Foreign Employment Board sent two teams abroad led by joint secretaries and other representatives to find new destinations, these teams only went on tours and returned without finding any specific markets.

He said that Nepalis are currently going to countries like Romania through the initiative of the private sector.

Dr. Gurung said, “It would be good if we could find out what kind of skills are needed in Romania – tractor driving or construction work? – and provide training in Nepal and send them through the government. That work has not been done.”

Although Nepal has signed labor agreements with some European countries including the UK and Germany, the expected benefits have not been realized. According to the agreement with the UK, only 45 nurses went for employment last year.

According to labor and immigration expert Rameshwar Nepal, the number of Nepalis going to Europe has been continuously increasing since 2023. Although employment in Europe is secure and the remuneration is good, workers have not been able to benefit due to the government's weak labor diplomacy.

Experts say that the limited UK agreement in the nursing sector has not been effective, and although agreements have been made with Germany and some Eastern European countries, their concrete impact has not been seen. They state that with agreements with the UAE, Qatar, and Malaysia also limited to paper, the growing attraction towards Europe, if not managed in time, will certainly lead to more complex problems.

What is the Government's Effort?

The government is making efforts to manage the growing foreign employment in Europe. However, it has not been successful. Currently, sending workers through institutional (manpower) channels to Europe is not allowed. Arbitrary fees are being collected from workers going through individual work permits.

To manage this, the government has been trying to send workers through manpower agencies for foreign employment, but demand letters from manpower agencies have not been attested so far.

The Ministry of Youth, Labor, and Employment had issued a procedure for attestation of demand letters. However, the procedure has not been implemented yet.

Ministry of Labor spokesperson Mira Acharya said that although the ministry is ready to find new labor destinations, some matters need to be handled by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. She stated that coordination is being done with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs for the attestation of demand letters from Europe.

According to her, the government has opened 178 countries for individual and 111 for institutional employment. Spokesperson Acharya said that the main responsibility for finding and promoting new markets lies with the private sector (manpower entrepreneurs).

Also Read About 70 percent of those going for foreign employment are unskilled

She clarified that the government will play the role of a regulator and facilitator, only attesting the demands brought by them within the legal framework. Currently, about 70 percent of workers going for foreign employment are unskilled.

Since it is difficult to find employment without skills in developed countries, the Gulf and Malaysia remain the main destinations for unskilled workers. The ministry has now adopted a policy of focusing on quality rather than quantity in foreign employment, according to spokesperson Acharya.

“The return from sending 10 highly skilled workers is greater than the remittance from sending 100 unskilled workers,” said Acharya. The ministry's conclusion is that skilled manpower can earn in 2 years what unskilled workers cannot earn in 5 years.

The ministry stated that it will take some time to sign labor agreements with new destination countries as the legal provisions of both countries and guarantees for worker safety are required. Discussions are currently underway for bilateral labor agreements with Mauritius, Seychelles, Maldives, and Sri Lanka, where potential is seen in the hospitality and tourism sectors.

The government is focusing its diplomatic efforts on transforming the compulsion of foreign employment into safe opportunities by urging entrepreneurs to find new markets and by ensuring workers are skilled before going abroad.

As the destination for Nepali workers shifts from the Gulf to Europe, it is evident that the government needs to take immediate diplomatic and policy steps to open institutional work permit channels, facilitate demand letter attestation, and control fraud.
